newsitem.title: UK: MINOR METALS - COBALT MAIN FOCUS, MARKET SLUGGISH.
newsitem.headline: MINOR METALS - COBALT MAIN FOCUS, MARKET SLUGGISH.

text.p: Minor metals largely remained in a torpor over the past week amid the lack of activity from consumers during the traditionally slow summer period.
But several traders believed the market was to move higher the fourth quarter of 1997 after finding support during the summer months.
"Normally you would expect prices to ease fairly substantially during the summer however this year the market has found underlying support from pockets of buying," one trader said.
"By October the market will see higher prices," another commented.

Most of this weeks attention focused on the start of U.S. stockpiled sales on Wednesday. A sale of 500,000 pounds of stockpiled material will be the first since the suspension in March following a legal dispute between the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center (DNSC) and Minor Metals Inc.
Stockpile cobalt sales were suspended in March because of two legal challenges by trading company Minor Metals Inc.

They were unhappy with Stockpile's inclusion of a domestic preference clause in sealed bids and other sales issues. Subsequently the U.S. District Court ruled in favour of the Stockpile, though traders said this prompted the DNSC to review its sales policies.
On Wednesday Minor Metals Inc said the latest sealed bid by the DNSC did not go far enough with its new independent assaying provision.
Minor Metals submitted a bid in Wednesday's offering which attached a

provision that offers to cover the cost of assaying all the drums using an approved Minor Metals Trade Association sampler appointed by the DNSC, but reserving the right to reject the lot "if the material does not conform to" the assay certificate.
It also asked for a refund for the amount paid for the rejected lot. The bid was for 88,888 pounds of cobalt at $18.88 a pound.

Traders during the week have speculated on the quality of the DNSC material. One suggested that the quality of the material was around 98.50 to 99.25 percent cobalt, below Russian graded ingots of 99.30 percent.
"The material is likely to be rondelles or granules and will not be pure enough to use in superalloys...the material is old stock, possibly dating back to the 1950s," the trader said.
"It probably came out of the former Belgium Congo nearly 50 years ago." he added. Cobalt used in superalloys is 99.80 percent minimum.

If the material is below the Russian 99.30 percent then it would be used in the manufacture of magnets and chemicals where lower grade cobalt is used extensively, traders said. Another trader said there were some good units of 99.40 per cent in the package but was unsure of the quantity.
Elsewhere, antimony drifted lower amid ample supply during the summer months.
"The market is drifting lower but will soon bottom out," one trader commented.
Expected consumer buying and re-stocking is expected to emerge during the fourth quarter of 1997.
Short supply kept vanadium firm. Traders noted that China was still not shipping large amounts of material.
Bismuth was stable but like other metals in the sector was looking for higher levels in the coming months. Any rise is likely to be capped at around $4.00 a pound, traders said.
